passages.t: Many rooms in My Father's house
passages.happening:
It is still the night of the last supper. Jesus has just told his friends that he is leaving, that one of them will betray him, and that Peter will deny him. Now he says, “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe in Me as well” (verse 1).

“In My Father’s house are many rooms” (verse 2). He is going there to prepare a place for them. “And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am” (verse 3).

“You know the way to the place where I am going” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Picture the room. The disciples have given up everything to follow Jesus. Now he says he is going where they cannot follow. They are frightened, confused and ashamed. His first words are not a rebuke. They are comfort.

‘My Father's house’ would bring two pictures to mind. One is a family home, where grown sons and their families often lived together, in rooms around a shared courtyard. The other is the temple, which Jesus had already called “My Father’s house” (2:16). Either way, the point is the same: there is room for them in the Father's family.

The Greek word for ‘rooms’, monai, means places to stay, dwellings. It comes from the verb ‘to remain’ or ‘abide’, one of John's favourite words. The King James Version says ‘many mansions’. That word came into English through the old Latin Bible's mansiones, and William Tyndale used it in his English New Testament in the 1520s. In older English a mansion simply meant a place to live, not a grand house. The promise is not about the size of the house. It is about being at home with God.

Later in this chapter Jesus uses the same Greek word again: he and the Father will come and make their ‘home’ with the one who loves him (verse 23). The room is not only waiting at the end. God comes to live with his people now.
passages.ot: The psalmist longed for this: “One thing I have asked of the LORD; this is what I desire: to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life” (Psalm 27:4). The best-loved psalm ends the same way: ‘I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever’ (Psalm 23:6).
passages.hard:
Is it wrong to be troubled? No. Jesus himself was troubled at Lazarus's tomb (11:33), facing his hour (12:27), and at the betrayal (13:21). When he says ‘Do not let your hearts be troubled’, he is not scolding frightened people. He is giving them a reason not to be ruled by fear: trust in God, and trust in him. The remedy he offers is not a feeling but a person, and a promise.

This chapter is read at many funerals. It does not answer every question about death. What it gives is a promise that is personal: ‘I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am.’ The heart of heaven, in these words, is not a place but being with Jesus.
passages.asks: Jesus' first answer to fear is not ‘try harder to be calm’. It is ‘believe in Me’. Ask what you are afraid of tonight, and what it would mean to trust him with it. And if you are grieving someone who trusted him, notice that the promise is personal: a place prepared, and a welcome from the one who prepared it.

passages.t: I am the way and the truth and the life
passages.happening:
Thomas speaks up. “Lord,” he says, “we do not know where You are going, so how can we know the way?” (verse 5).

Jesus answers, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (verse 6).

“If you had known Me, you would know My Father as well. From now on you do know Him and have seen Him” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Thomas is honest. He does not pretend to understand. Jesus does not scold him for the question. He answers it, and the answer is one of the best-known sentences in the Bible.

This is the sixth of the seven ‘I am’ sayings in John, each with a picture (6:35, 8:12, 10:7, 10:11, 11:25, 14:6, 15:1). Each takes something people cannot live without and says: this is what I am for you. Thomas asked for a road. Jesus says: I am the road.

‘The way’ was a familiar picture in Jewish teaching for how to live before God. The first Christians were even called followers of ‘the Way’ (Acts 9:2). ‘Truth’ in John means what is real and can be trusted, the truth about God. ‘Life’ means the life of God himself, eternal life, which begins now.

The church confesses these words as they stand. They claim that Jesus is not one guide among many, pointing toward God from a distance. He is himself the way to the Father, because he is the truth about God and the life of God come among us. Whoever comes to the Father comes through him. The apostles said the same in Jerusalem: “Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).
passages.ot: Isaiah pictured a road home for God's people: “And there will be a highway called the Way of Holiness” (Isaiah 35:8). The psalms ask God again and again to teach his way. Jesus says that the way the prophets longed for is not a road at all, but a person.
passages.hard:
Is it arrogant to say that no one comes to the Father except through Jesus? Many thoughtful people hear it that way, and the question deserves an honest answer, not a shrug.

Notice first when it is said. Jesus says it on the night before he dies, to frightened friends who have just asked how to find their way. It is offered as comfort, that there is a way to God, and that he is it. It is not said in scorn of anyone, and it gives no one leave to look down on people of other faiths or of none. Jesus is about to lay down his life for the world.

Notice also what it claims and what it does not. It says that whoever comes to the Father comes through Christ. It does not say that Christians know the fate of every person who never heard his name. Christians hold more than one view about that, and each takes Scripture seriously. On this site, the answers ‘Is Jesus really the only way to God?’ and ‘What about those who never heard of Jesus?’ set those views out fairly. These notes take no side among them.

And notice what the claim rests on. If Jesus were only a human teacher, it would be arrogant. John's whole book argues that he is more: the Word who was with God and was God (1:1). Coming to the Father through him is coming to God through God.
passages.asks: Thomas asked an honest question and got an answer worth everything. Ask what honest question about Jesus you have been afraid to say out loud. And ask whether you are treating Jesus as one helpful road among many, or as the way, the truth and the life.

passages.t: Whoever has seen Me has seen the Father
passages.happening:
Philip says, “Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us” (verse 8).

Jesus replies, “Philip, I have been with you all this time, and still you do not know Me? Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father” (verse 9). He is in the Father, and the Father is in him. The words he speaks and the works he does are the Father's (verse 10). If they cannot believe his word, “at least believe on account of the works themselves” (verse 11).

Then a great promise: “whoever believes in Me will also do the works that I am doing. He will do even greater things than these, because I am going to the Father” (verse 12). “And I will do whatever you ask in My name, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask Me for anything in My name, I will do it” (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
Philip's request is a deep one. To see God was the highest hope of any believer. Jesus' answer is astonishing: you have already been looking at him. Everything they have seen Jesus do, feeding, healing, raising, washing feet, is what the Father is like.

Notice that Jesus welcomes a faith that needs reasons. If his words are not enough, he says, look at the works. He does not ask for blind belief.

To ask ‘in My name’ meant more than adding words to the end of a prayer. In that world, a person sent in someone's name acted for him and carried his authority. To ask in Jesus' name is to ask as his people, for what he wants, so that the Father is glorified.
passages.ot: Moses once asked, “Please show me Your glory” (Exodus 33:18). God answered, “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live” (Exodus 33:20). John has already said, ‘No one has ever seen God’, but the Son ‘has made Him known’ (1:18). Philip is standing where Moses could not stand.
passages.hard:
Does ‘whatever you ask in My name’ mean Jesus will give us anything we want if we believe hard enough? A skeptic can fairly point to prayers that were not answered: the sick child who died, the marriage that ended. Some teachers have claimed that faith always brings health and money, and have blamed people when it did not. That is not what this passage teaches.

Read it in its setting. ‘In My name’ means as his people, for his purposes. The goal is stated in the same breath: ‘so that the Father may be glorified in the Son’. The First Letter of John puts it plainly: “If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us” (1 John 5:14). Within a few hours Jesus himself will ask for the cup to pass and accept that it will not (Mark 14:36). So most Christians read this as a call to bold prayer to a Father who listens, not as a key to make God do what we want. The notes on Mark 11 and Matthew 7 say the same.

And what are the ‘greater things’? Not bigger miracles than Jesus did; no one has done that. Most Christians read it as the wider reach of the work after Jesus returned to the Father and sent the Spirit. Jesus worked in one small land; his followers carried the good news to the nations. On the first day the church preached, ‘about three thousand were added to the believers’ (Acts 2:41).
passages.asks: Philip wanted to see God, and Jesus said: look at me. If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus, at the towel, the bread and the cross. Ask what picture of God you carry that does not look like him. And when you pray, ask whether you are asking for what he wants, in his name, or only for what you want, with his name added.

passages.t: Another Advocate, the Spirit of truth
passages.happening:
“If you love Me, you will keep My commandments” (verse 15). Jesus promises to ask the Father, and the Father “will give you another Advocate to be with you forever” (verse 16): the Spirit of truth. The world cannot receive him, because it does not see him or know him. “But you do know Him, for He abides with you and will be in you” (verse 17).

“I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you” (verse 18). Soon the world will not see him, but they will. “Because I live, you also will live” (verse 19).

Another Judas, not Judas Iscariot, asks why Jesus will show himself to them and not to the world (verse 22). Jesus answers, “If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word. My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our home with him” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The Greek word behind ‘Advocate’ is paraklētos. It means someone called to stand beside you. It was often used for someone who speaks for you in a court, a supporter or advocate. English Bibles have chosen different words, and each catches part of its meaning: Advocate, Helper, Comforter, Counselor. The Berean Standard Bible says ‘Advocate’. The King James Version says ‘Comforter’.

Jesus says ‘another’ Advocate. That means Jesus has been the first. All the help and closeness the disciples have had from him, the Spirit will now give, and give from within. The First Letter of John uses the same word for Jesus himself: “we have an advocate before the Father, Jesus Christ, the Righteous One” (1 John 2:1).

The Spirit is spoken of as a person, not a force. He teaches, reminds, testifies and guides (14:26, 15:26, 16:13). The Nicene Creed, in the older English wording printed on this site, confesses him as ‘the Lord and Giver of Life’, ‘who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified’.

‘Orphans’ is a strong word. In that world a disciple whose teacher died could feel orphaned. Jesus will not leave them that way.

This Judas is called ‘Judas son of James’ in Luke's list of the Twelve (Luke 6:16). Many think he is the one Matthew and Mark call Thaddaeus.
passages.ot: The prophets promised that God would one day put his own Spirit inside his people: “And I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27). Jeremiah said God would write his law on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). And the Law calls God the protector of orphans; the psalm says, “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation” (Psalm 68:5).
passages.hard:
Does ‘If you love Me, you will keep My commandments’ mean God's love depends on how well we obey? No. Jesus loved them first, ‘to the very end’ (13:1). Obedience is how love answers, not how love is earned. And the commandment he has just given is to love one another (13:34).

Why can the world not receive the Spirit? In John, ‘the world’ often means people organized against God, not the earth or any one nation. God still loves that world (3:16). It cannot receive the Spirit because it will not see or know him. That can change. The Spirit is about to be poured out on people who did not yet know him.
passages.asks: ‘I will not leave you as orphans.’ Some people hear those words with special force: anyone who lost a parent young, or grew up without a father, or feels alone in the world. Let them stand as the promise they are. Ask where you feel left alone. Jesus promises not only a place later, but company now: the Spirit with you, and the Father and the Son making their home with you.

passages.happening:
Jesus has said all this while still with them. “But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in My name, will teach you all things and will remind you of everything I have told you” (verse 26).

“Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled; do not be afraid” (verse 27).

He reminds them that he said he was going away and coming back. “If you loved Me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I” (verse 28). He tells them now, so that when it happens they will believe (verse 29). The prince of this world is coming, but he has no claim on Jesus (verse 30). Jesus does what the Father commanded, so that the world may know he loves the Father. “Get up! Let us go on from here” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
‘Peace’, shalom in Hebrew, was the everyday Jewish greeting and goodbye. It meant more than calm. It meant wholeness, things being right with God and with others. Jesus takes the ordinary goodbye and fills it. His peace is not the world's kind.

The Roman world spoke proudly of the peace Rome had brought, a peace kept by armies. Within hours the disciples would see that peace at work in a crucifixion. Jesus' peace is the opposite: given, not enforced, and paid for by himself.

‘Will remind you of everything I have told you’ matters for how we got the Gospels. Jesus promised that the Spirit would help the disciples remember and understand his words. John twice says that the disciples understood things only later, after Jesus rose (2:22, 12:16).

“Get up! Let us go on from here” sounds like the end of the talk, yet Jesus keeps speaking for three more chapters. Some think they rose and walked, and he taught them on the way. Others think the talks were gathered together. The text does not say.
passages.ot: The prophets promised a ruler of peace: “And He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6). Isaiah also said, “You will keep in perfect peace the steadfast of mind, because he trusts in You” (Isaiah 26:3). And the priests' blessing ended, ‘may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace’ (Numbers 6:26).
passages.hard:
If ‘the Father is greater than I’, is the Son less than God? This question is old and serious. In the early 300s a teacher named Arius said that the Son had a beginning and was not God in the same way as the Father, and his followers pointed to verses like this. Jehovah's Witnesses today read the verse the same way: the Father is greater, so the Son is not equal to God. They are sincere, and they deserve a patient answer, not scorn.

The church answered at the Council of Nicaea in 325. The Nicene Creed, in the older English wording printed on this site, confesses the Son as ‘very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father’. The Athanasian Creed, also printed on this site, says the Son is ‘equal to the Father, as touching his Godhead; and inferior to the Father, as touching his Manhood’. This is what the creeds bind all Christians to confess.

So how do Christians read ‘greater’? Many follow Augustine: Jesus speaks as the Son who took ‘the form of a servant’ (Philippians 2:7). In his human lowliness, about to die, he is less than the Father; in his nature as God, he is equal. Others add that the Father is the source of the Son, who is eternally from him, without being greater in being. The setting fits both: Jesus tells them to rejoice that he is going back to the Father, to the glory he had ‘before the world existed’ (17:5). And the same chapter says, ‘Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father’ (verse 9). At the end of the book Thomas will call him ‘My Lord and my God’ (20:28).
passages.asks:
‘Do not be afraid’ is not a rebuke of people who live with anxiety, panic or fear. Those are real struggles of body and mind, and they need care, not blame. Jesus said these words to friends who were rightly afraid, on the worst night of their lives, and he gave them his peace, not a lecture. Getting help is not a lack of faith. A doctor, a counselor, medicine, one trusted person who will stay. If you have reached the place where you are not sure you want to be here at all, tell someone today, and in the United States you can call or text 988 right now.

Ask what peace the world has offered you, and what it cost. Jesus' peace is a gift. You do not have to earn it, and you do not have to feel it first to receive it.
